title: Abba Chanan (tanna of a baraita)
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: Hyman describes him as a disciple of Rabbi Eliezer who always spoke in his name, as in Yevamot 64a, Sotah 14a, Bava Batra 119a and 130a, Sanhedrin 17a, Mekhilta Mishpatim ch. 3, Sifrei Naso 23, 66, 85, 128, Shelach 5, 8, 11, Korach 39. In several places we find that he spoke in the name of Rabbi Elazar, as in Yoma 3b, Yevamot 48b and 95b, Mekhilta Bo ch. 7, Mishpatim ch. 20, but Hyman proposes that in all of these one should read Rabbi Eliezer, since he was a colleague of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri (who was a disciple of Rabbi Tarfon), as in Nazir 45a, where Abba Hanan said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer – Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says – Abba Hanan said to him: by your own words, Sotah will prove it. Likewise we find that he spoke in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua, as in Niddah 29a.

We also find that he disagrees with Rabbi Yonatan in Mekhilta Mishpatim ch. 3, and there in ch. 12 with Rabbi Yoshiyah, and so it is cited in Bava Batra 119b. Hyman considers it without doubt that this is how the arrangers of the Talmud and the Mekhilta ordered it.

Likewise Rav Sherira Gaon wrote in his Iggeret, part 1, ch. 2, that he was in the generation of Rabbi Yishmael, the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, and of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha. Sometimes he is called Abba Hanin, as in Zevachim 4a.
He is mentioned only once on his own, in Gittin 56b, where he expounded "Who is like You, mighty (chasin)" — “who is like You, mighty and unyielding”.

notes.text: Hyman proposes Eliezer rather than Elazar by chronology. In the final homily, kasheh describes divine strength/endurance. Gittin56b continues by explaining divine silence at blasphemy; Hyman omits that continuation here.

The consulted Nazir 45a names Abba Chanan reporting Eliezer, followed by Shimon Shezuri; the Sotah objection continues on 45b. This does not independently verify every proposed Elazar-to-Eliezer substitution. Gittin 56b directly supports the strength-and-endurance homily, whose following explanation Hyman omits; his always, only-once and arrangement claims remain his.
